q: Solve the system: \(\begin{cases}3x + 2y = 1\\ x + 3y = 5\end{cases}\)
steps: Eliminate one variable: multiply the equations so the \(x\) (or \(y\)) coefficients match, then subtract.
Solving gives \(y = 2\); substitute back to get \(x = -1\).
Check in BOTH original equations: \(3(-1) + 2(2) = 1\) ✓

traps.why: Variables swapped — state the answer in the same (x, y) order as the system.
Sign error during elimination — subtracting equations flips every sign of the second equation, not just one term.

q: Solve the system: \(\begin{cases}x + 3y + 4z = -7\\ y + 3z = -5\\ z = -2\end{cases}\)
steps: Use row reduction: subtract rows to reach triangular form.
The last equation gives \(z=-2\); back-substitute upward.
Then \(y=1\) and finally \(x=-2\).

traps.why: y and z swapped during back-substitution — label each value as you find it.
Sign slip in the final back-substitution for x — move every known term across with its sign flipped.

steps: Let \(a\) = adult tickets, \(c\) = child tickets: \(a + c = 57\) and \(10a + 6c = 446\).
From the first equation \(c = 57 - a\); substitute into the second.

traps.why: Answer swapped — after solving, match each number back to its variable and its meaning.
The ticket-count equation and the money equation are different constraints — both must hold at once.

q: Which matrix is in reduced row echelon form (RREF)? \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\)
steps: RREF needs all four: leading entry of each nonzero row is 1; each leading 1 is the ONLY nonzero entry in its column; leading 1s move right as you go down; zero rows are at the bottom.
The correct matrix satisfies all four conditions.

traps.why: That is REF but not RREF — there is a nonzero entry ABOVE a leading 1. RREF requires zeros above and below each pivot.
A leading entry other than 1 disqualifies RREF — pivots must be scaled to 1.
A zero row sitting above a nonzero row violates echelon form — zero rows go last.

q: What single row operation transforms \(\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{array}\right]\) into \(\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{array}\right]\)?
steps: Row 1 is unchanged, so the operation acted on row 2.
The leading entry went from \(2\) to \(0\): we subtracted \(2\) copies of row 1.
Check another column to confirm the same multiple was used throughout.

traps.why: Adding would make the leading entry grow, not vanish — check the sign by what happened to column 1.
A swap changes BOTH rows — row 1 is identical in both matrices, so no swap occurred.

q: How many solutions does this system have? \(\begin{cases}x + y = -5\\ 2x - y = 1\end{cases}\)
steps: Compare the rows: is one left side a multiple of the other?
Here the left sides are NOT proportional, so the lines cross exactly once.
Conclusion: exactly one solution.

traps.why: Test proportionality of the FULL rows: left sides AND right side. Proportional left + matching right = infinite; proportional left + mismatched right = none; non-proportional left = unique.
Check whether the constant column follows the same multiple as the coefficients.

steps: The second row's left side is \(3\times\) the first row's.
For the rows to be the same equation (infinitely many solutions), the right side must scale the same way: \(h = 3\cdot-2 = -6\).
Any other \(h\) makes the system inconsistent (no solution).

traps.why: h must be k times the first right-hand side, not equal to it — the whole row scales.
Watch the sign of the multiplier k when scaling the constant.

q: Solve, expressing the solution set with a free parameter: \(\begin{cases}x + 2y = -4\\ 2x + 4y = -8\end{cases}\)
steps: Row 2 is \(2\times\) row 1 — only ONE independent equation, so one variable is free.
Let \(y = t\) (the free variable).
Then \(x = -4 - 2t\): every choice of \(t\) gives a solution.

traps.why: Proportional rows with MATCHING constants mean the same line twice — infinitely many solutions, not none. "No solution" needs mismatched constants.
That is one point on the solution line (t = 0), but the solution SET is the whole line — express it with the parameter.

q: Find the rank of \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 3 \\ 2 & -6 & 6 \\ -1 & 3 & -3\end{bmatrix}\).
steps: Row reduce and count the nonzero rows (equivalently, the pivots).
Every row is a multiple of the first — one independent row.

traps.why: Count pivots AFTER reducing — rows that look different can still be multiples of each other.
Do not stop reducing early; a row of zeros only appears once elimination is complete.
